lessons.title: Vowel Harmony
lessons.explanation: Turkish has vowel harmony: suffixes change their vowels to match the last vowel of the stem. There are two groups: back vowels (a, ı, o, u) and front vowels (e, i, ö, ü). A suffix with 'e' becomes 'a' after back vowels; a suffix with 'i' becomes 'ı', 'u', or 'ü' depending on the stem.
examples: ev + de = evde (in the house) — front vowel
araba + da = arabada (in the car) — back vowel
gel + iyor = geliyor (is coming) — front vowel
bak + ıyor = bakıyor (is looking) — back vowel
lessons.tip: Vowel harmony is the key to Turkish. Once you learn a suffix pattern, you just apply the matching vowel.

quiz.question: Turkish vowel harmony means that suffixes must match the __ of the stem.
What does 'arabada' mean?

lessons.title: SOV Order and Suffixes
lessons.explanation: Turkish is SOV (Subject-Object-Verb). The verb goes LAST. Turkish is agglutinative — many suffixes are stacked onto one word to express meaning. Example: evlerimizde = ev+ler+imiz+de = house+plural+our+in = 'in our houses'.
examples: Ben kitap okuyorum. (Ben = I, kitap = book, okuyorum = am reading)
O elma yiyor. (He/she is eating an apple.)
Biz okula gidiyoruz. (We are going to school.)
evlerimizde (in our houses) — 4 suffixes on one word
lessons.tip: In Turkish you can often express a whole English sentence with one heavily suffixed verb.

quiz.question: What is the word order of Turkish sentences?

lessons.title: Personal Suffixes on Verbs
lessons.explanation: Turkish verbs conjugate with personal suffixes added at the end (after tense suffixes). Suffixes: -(y)ım/im/um/üm (I), -sın/sin/sun/sün (you sg.), — (he/she/it has no suffix), -(y)ız/iz/uz/üz (we), -sınız/siniz/sunuz/sünüz (you pl./formal), -lar/ler (they).
examples: Ben gidiyorum. (I am going.) — gid+iyor+um
Sen gidiyorsun. (You are going.) — gid+iyor+sun
O gidiyor. (He/she is going.) — gid+iyor
Biz gidiyoruz. (We are going.) — gid+iyor+uz
lessons.tip: The subject pronoun is often omitted in Turkish because the verb suffix shows who is doing the action.

quiz.question: What suffix marks 1st person singular in Turkish present tense?

lessons.title: Cases — Locative, Dative, Ablative
lessons.explanation: Turkish nouns take case suffixes. Locative (-da/-de/-ta/-te): at/in/on. Dative (-(y)a/-(y)e): to/toward. Ablative (-dan/-den/-tan/-ten): from/away from. All follow vowel harmony.
examples: evde (at home) — locative
okula (to school) — dative
şehirden (from the city) — ablative
masada (on the table) — locative
İstanbul'a (to Istanbul) — dative
lessons.tip: The key cases to learn first: -de (in/at), -e (to), -den (from). They're enough for most basic conversations.

quiz.question: What does the Turkish suffix -da/-de express?

lessons.title: Tenses — Present Continuous and Simple
lessons.explanation: Turkish present continuous: verb stem + -iyor + personal suffix (with vowel harmony). Simple present (habitual/general truth): verb stem + -er/-ar/-ir/-ur (etc.) + personal suffix.
examples: Kitap okuyorum. (I am reading a book.) — -iyor
Her gün kitap okurum. (I read a book every day.) — -r (simple present)
Şimdi yiyor. (He/she is eating now.) — -iyor
Genellikle erken kalkarım. (I usually wake up early.) — -r
lessons.tip: Use -iyor for ongoing actions; use -r for habits, facts, and schedules.

quiz.question: Which suffix forms the present continuous in Turkish?

lessons.title: Accusative Case — Definite Direct Objects
lessons.explanation: When a direct object is definite (specific/known), Turkish marks it with the accusative suffix -(y)i/-ı/-u/-ü, chosen by four-way vowel harmony. Indefinite direct objects take no suffix at all.
examples: Kitabı okuyorum. (I am reading the book.) — definite, accusative -ı
Bir kitap okuyorum. (I am reading a book.) — indefinite, no suffix
Elmayı yedim. (I ate the apple.) — definite
Kapıyı açtı. (He/she opened the door.) — definite
lessons.tip: If the object is 'the X' (specific/known), add the accusative suffix; if it's just 'a X' (any one), leave it bare.

quiz.question: When does a Turkish direct object take the accusative suffix?
What is the accusative form of 'elma' (apple)?

lessons.title: Plural Suffix -lar/-ler and Vowel Harmony
lessons.explanation: Turkish forms plurals by adding -lar (after back vowels: a, ı, o, u) or -ler (after front vowels: e, i, ö, ü) to the noun, following two-way vowel harmony. The plural suffix comes before any case suffixes: evler (houses), evlerde (in the houses).
examples: ev → evler (house → houses) — front vowel
araba → arabalar (car → cars) — back vowel
kitap → kitaplar (book → books) — back vowel
göz → gözler (eye → eyes) — front vowel
lessons.tip: Choose -lar or -ler by checking only the LAST vowel of the noun, the same rule as all Turkish vowel harmony.

quiz.question: Which plural suffix follows 'araba' (car)?
What is the plural of 'göz' (eye)?

lessons.title: Question Particle mi/mı/mu/mü
lessons.explanation: Turkish yes/no questions are formed with the separate question particle mi (and its vowel-harmony variants mı, mu, mü), written as a separate word placed after the word being questioned, usually the verb: Geliyor musun? (Are you coming?).
examples: Geliyor musun? — Are you coming?
Bu kitap senin mi? — Is this book yours?
Öğretmen misin? — Are you a teacher?
Yemek güzel mi? — Is the food good?
lessons.tip: The question particle mi/mı/mu/mü is a separate word (with a space before it) and follows four-way vowel harmony like the accusative suffix.

quiz.question: How is a Turkish yes/no question typically formed?
options: With a separate question particle mi/mı/mu/mü

quiz.question: Which form of the question particle follows 'güzel' (front vowel e)?

lessons.title: Postpositions and Case Interactions
lessons.explanation: Turkish postpositions come AFTER the noun (like Japanese). Some require a specific case: için (for) uses nominative, ile (with) uses nominative, göre (according to) uses dative, önce (before) uses ablative.
examples: Senim için (for you) — için + nominative
arkadaşımla (with my friend) — ile attached as suffix
sana göre (according to you) — göre + dative
yemekten önce (before the meal) — önce + ablative
lessons.tip: Learn postpositions together with their required case — 'için + nominative' as one unit.

quiz.question: What case does 'için' (for) require in Turkish?

lessons.title: Past Tense (-di)
lessons.explanation: The Turkish definite past tense (-di) is added directly to the verb stem, with four-way vowel harmony and consonant devoicing after voiceless consonants (using t instead of d): geldi (came), gitti (went, t devoicing), baktı (looked).
examples: Dün geldim. — I came yesterday.
O gitti. — He/she went.
Baktık. — We looked.
Sen ne yaptın? — What did you do?
lessons.tip: After voiceless consonants (p, ç, t, k, s, ş, h, f), -di becomes -ti (devoicing) — e.g., gitti, not gitdi.

quiz.question: Which suffix marks the Turkish definite past tense?
Why does 'gitti' use -ti instead of -di?
options: Consonant devoicing after a voiceless stem

lessons.title: Future Tense (-ecek/-acak)
lessons.explanation: The Turkish future tense suffix is -ecek (after front vowels) or -acak (after back vowels), added to the verb stem before the personal suffix: gideceğim (I will go) — note the k softens to ğ before a vowel-initial suffix.
examples: Yarın geleceğim. — I will come tomorrow.
O okuyacak. — He/she will study/read.
Biz gideceğiz. — We will go.
Ne yapacaksın? — What will you do?
lessons.tip: Watch for consonant softening: the k of -ecek/-acak becomes ğ before a suffix starting with a vowel (geleceğim, not gelecekim).

quiz.question: Which suffix marks the Turkish future tense after a back-vowel stem?
What happens to the final k of -ecek/-acak before a vowel-initial suffix?

lessons.title: Possessive Suffixes
lessons.explanation: Turkish nouns take possessive suffixes to show ownership, agreeing with the possessor's person: -(i)m (my), -(i)n (your), -(s)i (his/her/its), -(i)miz (our), -(i)niz (your pl.), -(leri) (their), all following vowel harmony: evim (my house), evin (your house), evi (his/her house).
examples: evim — my house
kitabın — your book
arabası — his/her car
okulumuz — our school
lessons.tip: Unlike English 'my house', Turkish marks possession on the NOUN itself with a suffix, and the possessor pronoun (benim, senin...) is often optional.

quiz.question: Which suffix means 'my' when attached to a noun?
What does 'arabası' mean?

lessons.title: Evidentiality — Direct vs. Reported Past
lessons.explanation: Turkish has two past tenses distinguished by whether you witnessed the event directly. Definite past (-di): you saw it happen. Inferential/reported past (-miş): you heard about it or inferred it.
examples: Dün geldi. (He came yesterday.) — -di, you witnessed this
Dün gelmiş. (He apparently came yesterday.) — -miş, you heard this
Çok uyumuşsun! (You've slept a lot!) — -miş, you inferred from evidence
Deprem oldu. (An earthquake happened.) — -di, reported as fact
lessons.tip: -miş is also used in fairy tales (like 'once upon a time') and when reporting hearsay.

quiz.question: Which Turkish past tense suffix marks events you didn't witness directly?

lessons.title: Conditional Mood (-se/-sa)
lessons.explanation: Turkish forms conditional clauses with the suffix -se (front vowels) or -sa (back vowels) attached to the verb stem, meaning 'if': gelirse (if he/she comes), giderse (if he/she goes). It combines with tense/aspect forms for hypotheticals: gitseydim (if I had gone).
examples: Yağmur yağarsa, evde kalırım. — If it rains, I will stay home.
Param olsa, seyahat ederim. — If I had money, I would travel.
Gitseydim, onu görürdüm. — If I had gone, I would have seen him/her.
Erken kalkarsan, treni yakalarsın. — If you wake up early, you'll catch the train.
lessons.tip: -se/-sa attaches directly to express 'if'; combine with -ydi (gitseydim) for unreal past conditionals like English 'if I had gone.'

quiz.question: Which suffix means 'if' in Turkish conditional sentences?
What does 'gitseydim' express?

lessons.title: Passive and Reflexive Voice Suffixes
lessons.explanation: Turkish marks passive voice with -il/-ıl/-ul/-ül (or -n after vowel-final stems): yazmak (to write) becomes yazılmak (to be written). Reflexive voice uses -in/-ın/-un/-ün (or -n): yıkamak (to wash) becomes yıkanmak (to wash oneself).
examples: Mektup yazıldı. — The letter was written. (passive)
Kapı açıldı. — The door was opened. (passive)
Çocuk yıkandı. — The child washed himself/herself. (reflexive)
O aynada süslendi. — He/she got dressed up in the mirror. (reflexive)
lessons.tip: Passive -il/-ıl/-ul/-ül removes the doer from focus; reflexive -in/-ın/-un/-ün shows the subject acts on themselves — both attach directly to the verb stem.

quiz.question: Which suffix marks the Turkish passive voice?
What does the reflexive suffix indicate?

lessons.title: Causative Voice
lessons.explanation: Turkish causative suffixes (variants like -dir/-tir, -t, -ir, -er, depending on the stem) turn a verb into 'make/have someone do something': yazmak (to write) becomes yazdırmak (to have someone write); yapmak (to do) becomes yaptırmak (to have something done). Some verbs stack multiple voice suffixes, such as passive plus causative.
examples: Mektubu yazdırdım. — I had the letter written (by someone).
Çocuğa yemek yedirdi. — He/she fed the child (made the child eat).
Evi yaptırıyoruz. — We are having the house built.
Saçını kestirdi. — He/she had his/her hair cut.
lessons.tip: Causative -dir-type suffixes answer 'who made this happen' — the person who actually performs the action becomes a secondary object, often marked with -e/-a (to) or -i/-ı (definite object).

quiz.question: What does the Turkish causative suffix express?
options: Making/having someone else do the action

quiz.question: In 'Saçını kestirdi', what does 'kestirdi' imply?
options: He had someone cut it for him
